name: Pork
note: Pork and anything made from pigs is haram.

name: Lard
note: Lard is pork fat and is haram.

name: Bacon
note: Bacon is pork unless the label clearly says turkey or beef "bacon" from a halal source.

name: Ham
note: Ham is pork unless clearly labelled as a halal turkey or chicken alternative.

name: Chorizo
note: Traditional chorizo is made from pork. Halal versions (chicken or beef) are labelled and certified.

name: Salami
note: Most salami and pepperoni in UK shops contain pork. Only eat halal-certified versions.

name: Pepsin
note: Commercial pepsin is almost always from pigs.

name: Alcohol
note: Added alcohol is avoided. Scholars differ on tiny carrier amounts, but added alcohol as an ingredient is generally treated as haram.

name: Wine
note: Wine is haram, including when used for cooking.

name: Beer
note: Alcoholic drinks are haram, including in batters and sauces.

name: Alcoholic drink flavouring
note: Some "rum flavour" products contain real rum; others are synthetic. Check with the maker.
from: Flavour that may be made with the drink itself.

name: Vanilla extract
note: Vanilla extract is made with alcohol. Many scholars allow it because the amount is tiny and it is not intoxicating in food; others avoid it. Vanilla flavouring, vanillin and vanilla pods are fine.

name: Wine vinegar
note: Most scholars hold that vinegar is halal even when made from wine, because the alcohol has changed into acid. Strict mode flags it.
from: Wine that has fully turned to vinegar.

name: Vinegar
from: Fermentation of alcohol into acetic acid.

name: Gelatine
note: Treated as haram when the source is not stated, because most gelatine in Europe is from pigs.
from: Animal skin and bones — in Europe mostly pork.

name: Beef gelatine
note: Only halal if the cattle were halal-slaughtered. Look for a halal logo.

name: Collagen
note: Halal if marine or from a halal-slaughtered animal.

name: Isinglass
note: Fish-derived, so halal. Used to clear some drinks.

name: Carmine (cochineal)
note: Most UK scholars and certifiers avoid it; some scholars permit it. Follows your insect setting.

name: L-cysteine
note: Halal only if fermented or from a halal source.
from: Feathers, pig bristles, hair, or fermentation.

name: Animal fat
note: Could be pork or non-halal meat. Avoid unless certified.

name: Suet
note: Only halal if from halal-slaughtered animals.

name: Tallow
note: Only halal if from halal-slaughtered animals. Also used in soaps.

name: Glycerine
note: Halal when vegetable glycerine; doubtful if not stated.
from: Plant oils, animal fat or synthetic.

name: Plant-based mono- and diglycerides
note: Halal when the label states a plant source.
terms: mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids (vegetable)
mono and diglycerides of vegetable fatty acids
mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids (plant)

name: Emulsifier (source not stated)
note: On its own the word "emulsifier" tells you little. Look at which emulsifier is named after it. Strict mode flags it.

name: Shellac
note: Most certifiers accept it. Strict mode flags it.

name: Keratin
note: Common in hair products. Doubtful unless a halal source is stated.

name: Lanolin
note: Most scholars treat wool-derived lanolin as halal. Used in vitamin D3 and cosmetics.
from: Sheep wool grease, taken without harm to the sheep.

name: Rennet
note: Animal rennet is only halal from halal-slaughtered calves. Microbial or vegetarian rennet is halal. Many cheeses do not say which.

name: Enzymes (unspecified)
note: Most food enzymes are microbial today, but animal ones exist. Doubtful when unspecified.

name: Cheese
note: Depends on the rennet. Many UK supermarket cheddars use microbial rennet and are labelled vegetarian; Parmesan and Grana Padano always use animal rennet.

name: Whey
note: Many scholars and certifiers accept whey even from animal-rennet cheese; others avoid it. Strict mode flags it.

name: Casein
note: Milk protein — halal. Strict mode flags it because some casein is made using animal rennet.

name: Beef
note: Halal only if slaughtered according to Islamic law. Look for a halal certification logo (e.g. HMC or HFA in the UK).

name: Lamb / mutton
note: Halal only if slaughtered according to Islamic law. Look for certification.

name: Chicken
note: Halal only if slaughtered according to Islamic law. Look for certification.

name: Turkey / duck
note: Halal only if slaughtered according to Islamic law. Look for certification.

name: Meat (unspecified)
note: Unspecified meat could include pork. Avoid unless certified.

name: Halal meat
note: Halal when genuinely certified. Check the certifier logo.

name: Fish
note: Fish is halal in all schools of thought.

name: Shellfish (prawns, crab, mussels)
note: Halal according to the Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools. In the Hanafi school only fish is permitted (prawns are debated among Hanafis), so the Hanafi setting marks these as doubtful.

name: Ginger ale / root beer
note: Ginger ale and root beer are soft drinks. Alcohol-free beer usually still has up to 0.5% alcohol, so strict mode flags these.
from: Soft drinks named after alcoholic drinks.

name: Additive group words
note: This word just names a group. The actual additive is listed after it.

name: Flavourings
note: Most flavourings are fine, but the word can hide alcohol carriers or animal sources. Strict mode flags it.
from: Plant, synthetic, and occasionally animal or alcohol-carried.

name: Yeast extract
note: Halal. Brewer's yeast is washed and transformed; most scholars accept it.

name: Fatty alcohols (cetyl, stearyl, cetearyl)
note: Despite the name, these are not drinking alcohol. They are solid, non-intoxicating waxes used to thicken creams, and are halal.
from: Waxy substances usually made from coconut or palm oil.

name: Benzyl alcohol
from: Synthetic preservatives, or found naturally in fruits.

name: Denatured alcohol (alcohol denat.)
note: Most scholars permit alcohol in products used on the skin, especially synthetic or industrial alcohol, because it is not being drunk. Some prefer to avoid it. Strict mode flags it.
from: Ethanol made undrinkable with additives, or synthetic.

name: Squalane (plant)
note: Squalane in cosmetics is almost always plant-based. Halal.

name: Squalene
note: Squalene can come from shark liver (halal in Sunni schools as it is from fish) or olives. Doubtful only for those who avoid shark.
from: Shark liver oil or olive oil.

name: Sodium tallowate
note: Made from beef or mutton fat, and occasionally pork. Doubtful unless the source is stated. Common in bar soap.

name: Placenta extract
note: Most scholars do not permit products from human placenta; animal placenta depends on the animal and its slaughter. Treated as doubtful.

name: Snail mucin
note: Snails are not eaten according to most scholars. Views differ on using their secretion on the skin; many consider it permissible because it is a secretion and not eaten. Treated as doubtful.

name: Hyaluronic acid
note: Almost always made by fermentation today, so halal. Strict mode flags it because an animal source is possible.
from: Usually bacterial fermentation; sometimes rooster combs.

name: Musk and ambergris
note: Musk was used and praised by the Prophet ﷺ, and most scholars consider it pure. Most musk today is synthetic.
from: Musk deer (natural) or synthetic; ambergris from whales.

name: Softgel capsule
note: Most soft capsules are made from gelatine. Look for "fish gelatine", "halal gelatine" or a vegetarian capsule. See "Is gelatine in medicine halal?" for scholars' views on medicines.
from: Usually gelatine from cattle, pigs or fish.

name: Heparin
note: Heparin is usually made from pigs. Most scholars permit it when medically needed and no alternative exists, based on necessity (darurah). Ask your doctor about alternatives if this matters to you.

name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
note: Lanolin-derived vitamin D3 is accepted by most scholars. Strict mode flags it because the source is not always stated.
from: Usually lanolin from sheep wool; sometimes fish oil or lichen.

name: Riboflavin (vitamin B2)
note: No animal source in normal food production.

name: Riboflavin-5'-phosphate
note: No animal source in normal food production.

name: Tartrazine
note: Synthetic. Some people avoid it for health reasons, not halal reasons.

name: Carmine / cochineal
note: Made from insects. Most UK scholars and certifiers treat it as not permissible; some scholars (notably in the Maliki school) permit it. Your insect setting controls how it is shown.

name: Indigo carmine (indigotine)
note: Despite the name, it is not made from cochineal insects.

name: Sulphite ammonia caramel
note: Made from sugar. The colour in most colas.

name: Carotenes (beta-carotene)
note: The colour itself is halal. Some powdered forms are coated in gelatin, so strict mode flags it.

name: Anthocyanins
note: Plant-derived. Grape-skin extract is not wine.

name: Titanium dioxide
note: Mineral. Banned as a food additive in the EU since 2022 for safety reasons; still allowed in Great Britain.

name: Silver
note: Used as decoration in small amounts.

name: Gold
note: Used as decoration in small amounts.

name: Sodium nitrite
note: Synthetic. Common in cured meats — the meat itself is what needs checking.

name: Lactic acid
note: Microbial. Not made from milk despite the name.

name: Ascorbyl palmitate
note: The fatty acid is usually from palm oil but can come from animal fat. Halal if plant-based.
from: Vitamin C combined with palmitic acid, a fatty acid.

name: Lecithins
note: Almost always plant-based; egg lecithin is also halal.
from: Soya, sunflower or rapeseed; rarely egg.

name: Tartaric acid
note: Most scholars accept it because it is fully transformed (istihalah) and contains no alcohol. Strict mode flags it.
from: Often a by-product of wine making; also synthetic.

name: Sodium tartrates
note: See E334. Strict mode flags it.

name: Potassium tartrates (cream of tartar)
note: See E334. Strict mode flags it.
from: Made from tartaric acid, often from wine sediment.

name: Metatartaric acid
note: See E334. Strict mode flags it.

name: Calcium tartrate
note: See E334. Strict mode flags it.

name: Agar
note: A common halal replacement for gelatin.

name: Glycerol (glycerine)
note: Halal when the label says vegetable glycerine; doubtful when the source is not stated.
from: Vegetable oils, animal fats, or synthetic.

name: Pectins
note: Plant-derived. A halal gelling agent used in many jams and sweets.

name: Gelatine
note: Treated as haram unless the pack states a halal source such as fish gelatine or halal-certified beef gelatine.
from: Animal skin and bones — in Europe mostly pork.

name: Ammonium phosphatides
note: Used in chocolate. Plant-based in practice.

name: Glycerol esters of wood rosins
note: The glycerol part can occasionally be animal-derived, so strict mode flags it.

name: Sodium, potassium and calcium salts of fatty acids
note: Halal only if the fatty acids are plant-based or from a halal animal.

name: Magnesium salts of fatty acids
note: Halal only if the fatty acids are plant-based or from a halal animal.

name: Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
note: One of the most common doubtful additives. Halal if the pack says plant/vegetable origin or is halal-certified or vegan.
from: Plant oils (usually palm) or animal fats including pork.
terms: mono and diglycerides of fatty acids
mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids

name: Acetic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
note: Same doubt as E471 — depends on the fat source.

name: Lactic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
note: Same doubt as E471 — depends on the fat source.

name: Citric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
note: Same doubt as E471 — depends on the fat source.

name: Mono- and diacetyl tartaric acid esters (DATEM)
note: Same doubt as E471 — depends on the fat source. Very common in bread.
from: Made from E471 and tartaric acid.

name: Sucrose esters of fatty acids
from: Sugar plus plant or animal fatty acids.

name: Sucroglycerides
from: Sugar plus plant or animal fats.

name: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids
from: Glycerol and fatty acids from plant or animal fats.

name: Polyglycerol polyricinoleate (PGPR)
note: The castor oil part is plant-based; the glycerol part can be animal-derived. Common in chocolate.

name: Propylene glycol esters of fatty acids
from: Fatty acids from plant or animal fats.

name: Sodium stearoyl-2-lactylate
note: Depends on the source of the stearic acid. Common in bread.
from: Stearic acid (plant or animal) and lactic acid.

name: Calcium stearoyl-2-lactylate
note: Depends on the source of the stearic acid.
from: Stearic acid (plant or animal) and lactic acid.

name: Sorbitan monostearate
note: Depends on the source of the stearic acid.
from: Sorbitol and stearic acid (plant or animal).

name: Sorbitan tristearate
note: Depends on the source of the stearic acid.
from: Sorbitol and stearic acid (plant or animal).

name: Sorbitan mono-oleate
from: Sorbitol and oleic acid (plant or animal).

name: Sorbitan monopalmitate
from: Sorbitol and palmitic acid (plant or animal).

name: Bone phosphate
note: Made from bones. Only halal if the bones come from a halal-slaughtered animal; the source is rarely stated.

name: Stearic acid (fatty acids)
note: Halal if plant-based. Also used in tablets and cosmetics.

name: Magnesium stearate
note: Common in tablets and supplements. Depends on the stearic acid source.
from: Stearic acid (plant or animal) and magnesium.

name: Disodium guanylate
note: Almost always from yeast or fermentation today. Strict mode flags it because an animal source is possible.
from: Usually yeast extract or fermentation; historically sardines or meat.

name: Disodium inosinate
note: Can be made from meat (including pork) or fish. Halal if the product is vegan/vegetarian-labelled or certified.

name: Disodium 5'-ribonucleotides
from: A mix of E627 and E631.

name: Glycine
note: Usually synthetic, but an animal (gelatin) source is possible.
from: Mostly synthetic; can be made from gelatin.

name: Beeswax
note: Bee products such as honey and wax are halal.

name: Shellac
note: It is a secretion (like honey), not the insect itself, and most certifiers accept it. Strict mode flags it.
from: Resin secreted by the lac insect.

name: L-cysteine
note: Halal if made by fermentation or from halal poultry feathers; the source is rarely stated. Found in some bread and bakery products.
from: Duck feathers, pig bristles, human hair, or fermentation.

name: Lysozyme
note: Egg-derived — halal. Used in some cheeses.

name: Triethyl citrate
note: A fully transformed ester, not alcohol. Strict mode flags it.
from: Made from citric acid and ethanol.

name: Ethanol (alcohol)
note: Added alcohol. Scholars differ on tiny carrier amounts in flavourings, but added ethanol is generally avoided.

name: Glyceryl triacetate (triacetin)
from: Glycerol (plant or animal) and acetic acid.

name: Propylene glycol
note: Synthetic. It is not alcohol in the sense that matters for halal.

name: Is Stunned Meat Halal?
note: Scholars differ. Many accept meat from animals stunned in a reversible way, as long as the animal is still alive at the moment of slaughter and the Islamic conditions are met. Others reject all stunning because some animals may die from it. In the UK, HFA accepts some reversible stunning, while HMC accepts no stunning.

name: Is Machine-Slaughtered Chicken Halal?
note: Scholars differ. Many hold that a rotating blade slaughter is acceptable if a Muslim operates it and says God's name, as happens in some certified plants. Many others — especially in the Hanafi school — require hand slaughter with God's name said for each bird, so they do not accept machine slaughter.

name: Is Kosher Meat Halal?
note: Scholars differ. Some permit kosher meat because the Qur'an allows the food of Jews and Christians and kosher slaughter is done by hand without stunning. Many others, especially Hanafi scholars, say it is not halal because God's name is not said over each animal. Kosher-certified foods can also contain wine or non-halal gelatine, so kosher is not the same as halal.
terms: is kosher the same as halal?

name: Is Supermarket Meat Halal?
note: Most contemporary scholars say ordinary supermarket meat in the UK, Europe and the US is not halal, because the slaughter method (often stunning, sometimes killing) and the slaughterer's religion cannot be confirmed. A minority permit it based on the Qur'an allowing the food of Christians and Jews. Buy meat labelled halal from a certifier you trust.
terms: is supermarket meat halal? (meat of the people of the book)
can muslims eat meat from tesco?
is non-halal meat allowed for muslims in europe?
can muslims eat meat slaughtered by christians?

name: Is Food With a Little Alcohol Halal?
note: Food cooked with wine, beer or spirits is not permitted according to most scholars, because alcoholic drinks are forbidden and cooking does not remove all the alcohol. Traces of alcohol that occur naturally (in bread, fruit or juice) or tiny amounts used as a flavouring carrier are treated differently, and many scholars permit them.
terms: is food with a little alcohol halal? (cooking with wine)
can muslims eat food cooked with wine?

name: Is Non-Alcoholic Beer Halal?
note: Scholars differ. Many advise avoiding alcohol-free beer and wine because they are made by producing an alcoholic drink and then removing the alcohol, often leave up to 0.5% behind, and imitate the drinking culture of alcohol. Some scholars permit genuine 0.0% drinks that cannot intoxicate.
terms: can muslims drink zero alcohol beer?

name: Is Soy Sauce Halal?
note: Naturally brewed soy sauce contains a little alcohol from fermentation, and some brands add alcohol as a preservative. Many scholars permit it because the alcohol is not intoxicating and is not from wine; others prefer to avoid it. Halal-certified soy sauces are widely available.

name: Is Kombucha Halal?
note: Kombucha is fermented tea that naturally contains a small amount of alcohol, usually under 0.5%. Many scholars permit it because it does not intoxicate and is made as a soft drink. Others advise caution, especially with home-brewed or "hard" kombucha, which can be much stronger.

name: Is Vanilla Extract Halal?
note: Vanilla extract is made by soaking vanilla in alcohol. Many scholars permit it in food because the amount is tiny and non-intoxicating, and the alcohol is usually not from wine. Others avoid it. Vanilla flavouring, vanillin, vanilla pods and alcohol-free extract are halal by all views.

name: Can Muslims Eat at Non-Halal Restaurants?
note: Many scholars permit eating vegetarian or fish dishes at a non-halal restaurant, provided they contain no alcohol or other haram ingredients. The main concerns are cross-contamination (shared fryers, grills and utensils) and alcohol in sauces. Meat is only halal if the restaurant uses certified halal meat.
terms: can muslims eat at non-halal restaurants?
can muslims eat at restaurants that serve pork?
is vegetarian food at non-halal restaurants halal?

name: Are Energy Drinks Halal?
note: Most energy drinks, coffee and tea are halal by their ingredients. Caffeine is not an intoxicant, and taurine in energy drinks is synthetic, not from animals. Some scholars discourage heavy energy-drink use because of health harm. Check individual flavours for colours such as carmine (E120).
terms: are energy drinks halal? (red bull, monster, prime)

name: Is Medicine With Gelatine Halal?
note: If a halal alternative exists (a vegetarian capsule or a different brand), most scholars say to choose it. Where a medicine containing pork gelatine is needed and there is no alternative, scholars widely permit it based on necessity (darurah). Some also argue gelatine is fully transformed (istihalah). Ask your pharmacist about gelatine-free options.
terms: can muslims take medicine with gelatin?

name: Is It Halal to Invest in Stocks?
note: Yes, investing in shares is halal according to most scholars, as long as the company's main business is halal and it passes Shariah screening — mainly low debt and very little income from interest or haram activities. Speculative day-trading with leverage is widely considered not permissible.
terms: is it halal to invest in stocks?

name: Is Crypto Halal?
note: Scholars differ. Many contemporary scholars and Shariah advisers accept buying and holding major cryptocurrencies as digital assets, provided they are not used for haram purposes. Others, including Egypt's Dar al-Ifta and Turkey's Diyanet, have said it is not permissible. Leveraged crypto trading and futures are widely considered haram.
terms: is crypto halal? bitcoin and cryptocurrency explained

name: Is It Halal to Invest in Gold?
note: Buying physical gold and taking possession of it is halal. Because gold is a "ribawi" item, Islamic law requires the exchange to be immediate. Gold ETFs are accepted by many scholars only if they are fully backed by allocated physical gold; leveraged XAUUSD trading through CFDs is widely considered haram.
terms: is it halal to invest in gold? (gold etfs and xauusd)
can muslims buy gold as an investment?

name: Is Forex Trading Halal or Haram?
note: Exchanging currencies is halal when both sides are delivered immediately (spot exchange). Most retail forex trading, however, uses leverage, CFDs and overnight interest, which the majority of scholars consider impermissible. "Islamic" swap-free accounts remove interest but scholars still differ on leveraged trading.
terms: is forex trading halal or haram?

name: Is a Mortgage Halal?
note: A conventional interest-based mortgage involves riba, which is forbidden, so most scholars say to avoid it. Islamic home finance (such as ijara or diminishing musharaka) is available in the UK and many Western countries. A minority view — including a 1999 opinion of the European Council for Fatwa and Research — permits a conventional mortgage for a family home in cases of real need.
terms: is a mortgage halal? conventional vs islamic mortgages
is it haram to buy a house with a mortgage?

name: Is It Halal to Open a Savings Account?
note: Keeping money in a bank is fine, but earning interest (riba) is forbidden. Choose an Islamic savings account, which pays an expected profit rate from permitted investments instead of interest. If you already have interest, most scholars advise giving it to charity without expecting reward, rather than keeping it.
terms: is it halal to open a savings account? (interest explained)
can muslims earn interest on savings?
what should i do with bank interest?

name: Is It Halal to Use a Credit Card?
note: Many scholars permit using a credit card if you always pay the full balance before any interest is charged, and never use it for cash withdrawals that carry interest. Signing an agreement that includes interest is disliked by some scholars, so a debit card or a Shariah-compliant card is the safest option.
terms: is it halal to use a credit card?

name: Is Klarna Halal?
note: Interest-free "pay in 3" or "pay in 30 days" plans are considered permissible by many scholars, because you pay the same price with no interest. Plans that charge interest, or late fees that work like interest, are not. To stay safe, only use interest-free options and always pay on time.
terms: is klarna halal? buy now pay later explained
is buy now pay later halal?

name: Is Student Finance Halal?
note: UK scholars differ. Student Finance loans charge interest linked to inflation, which many scholars consider riba and so impermissible. Others permit them because repayment works more like a graduate tax — you only repay above an income threshold and the rest is written off. The UK government has long promised a Shariah-compliant alternative.
terms: is student finance halal? uk student loans explained

name: Is Insurance Halal?
note: Many scholars consider conventional insurance problematic because of excessive uncertainty (gharar), gambling-like features and interest-based investments. Takaful — cooperative Islamic insurance — is the preferred alternative. Where insurance is required by law, such as car insurance in the UK, most scholars permit it out of necessity.
terms: is insurance halal? car, home and life insurance

name: Is the Lottery Haram?
note: Yes — gambling, including the lottery, scratch cards, sports betting and casino games, is haram. The Qur'an explicitly forbids maysir (gambling) alongside alcohol. Most scholars also prohibit raffles where you pay for a chance to win, and "matched betting", because they rely on gambling contracts.
terms: is the lottery haram? gambling, betting and raffles

name: Are Premium Bonds Halal?
note: UK scholars differ. Your capital is never lost, which some scholars say means it is not gambling. However, the prizes are paid from the interest the pool would have earned and are distributed by chance, which many scholars say combines riba with a lottery. Many Muslims avoid Premium Bonds for this reason.

name: Is Dropshipping Halal?
note: Dropshipping can be halal if structured correctly. The concern is selling something you do not yet own, which a hadith forbids. Scholars say it becomes permissible if you act as the supplier's agent for a commission, take a pre-order and then buy, or use a salam-style arrangement — and of course the products themselves must be halal.

name: Is It Halal to Work in a Bank?
note: Scholars say roles that directly write, witness or manage interest-based loans are not permitted, based on the hadith cursing those who record riba. Jobs that are not directly involved in interest — such as IT, cleaning, security or Islamic banking — are considered permissible by many scholars.
terms: is it halal to work in a bank?
is working in a bank haram?
can muslims work at a bank?

name: Is It Halal to Work Somewhere That Sells Alcohol or Pork?
note: Scholars distinguish between direct and indirect involvement. Serving, selling or delivering alcohol is not permitted according to most scholars, because the Prophet ﷺ cursed those who carry and sell it. Working in a shop or restaurant where you are not handling alcohol or pork directly is permitted by many scholars, especially where other work is hard to find.
terms: is it halal to work somewhere that sells alcohol or pork?
can muslims work at a supermarket that sells alcohol?
is it halal to work at mcdonald's?
can muslims work in a restaurant that serves pork?

name: Are Vaccines Halal?
note: Scholars widely permit vaccines, including those containing porcine gelatine, when there is no alternative, because protecting life and health is a priority in Islam. The British Fatwa Council has said the children's nasal flu vaccine is permissible. Where a gelatine-free version exists — such as for MMR in the UK — scholars recommend asking for it.
terms: are vaccines halal? (porcine gelatine in vaccines)

name: Is Organ Donation Halal?
note: Scholars differ. Many — including bodies such as the European Council for Fatwa and Research — permit organ donation, during life or after death, because saving a life is highly rewarded. Others prohibit it because of the sanctity of the body. In England, you can record your decision and your faith beliefs on the NHS Organ Donor Register.
terms: is it haram to donate organs after death?

name: Is Blood Donation Halal?
note: Yes. Scholars widely permit donating blood, as it saves lives, causes no lasting harm and the body replaces it. Receiving a blood transfusion is also permitted. It is best not to sell blood.

name: Are Tattoos Haram?
note: Permanent tattoos are haram according to the majority of scholars, based on a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ cursed those who tattoo and those who get tattooed. Henna and temporary tattoos that do not go under the skin are permitted. If you had a tattoo before, most scholars say you do not have to remove it if removal is harmful, and your prayers and wudu are valid.
terms: is it haram to get a tattoo?

name: Are Piercings Halal?
note: Ear piercing for women is permitted by all schools; it was known at the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Nose piercing for women is permitted by most scholars where it is a normal form of adornment. Piercings for men, and body piercings beyond the ears and nose, are discouraged or prohibited by most scholars because they imitate the opposite sex or cause harm.
terms: is it haram to get a nose piercing?
can muslim men pierce their ears?

name: Is It Halal to Dye Your Hair?
note: Yes. Dyeing hair is permitted and was encouraged for grey hair — the Prophet ﷺ recommended henna. Scholars differ on dyeing hair pure black: many discourage or prohibit it, based on a hadith, while others permit it. Hair dye does not affect wudu because it colours the hair rather than coating it.
terms: is it halal to dye your hair?
is it haram to dye your hair black?

name: Is Nail Polish Halal?
note: Wearing nail polish is permitted, but regular polish forms a waterproof layer, so wudu made while wearing it is not valid according to most scholars — it must be removed before wudu. So-called "breathable" or "halal" nail polish claims to let water through; some scholars accept products that genuinely pass water, others remain cautious. Henna is fine.
terms: is nail polish halal? (and breathable nail polish)
can you pray with nail polish on?

name: Is Plucking or Threading Eyebrows Haram?
note: Most scholars say shaping the eyebrows by plucking or threading is not permitted, based on a hadith cursing "an-namisah" — the one who plucks eyebrows. Many scholars permit removing hair between the eyebrows (a monobrow) or stray hairs that are unusual, and some permit a married woman to tidy her brows for her husband.
terms: is plucking or threading eyebrows haram?
is it haram to pluck eyebrows?
is it halal to remove hair between eyebrows?
can muslim women thread their eyebrows?

name: Is Perfume With Alcohol Halal?
note: Many contemporary scholars permit wearing perfume that contains alcohol, because it is not being drunk and the alcohol in perfume is usually synthetic or industrial, not wine. Others consider alcohol impure and prefer alcohol-free perfume, especially for prayer. Alcohol-free attar and oil perfumes avoid the question.
terms: can muslims wear perfume with alcohol?
can you pray wearing alcohol-based perfume?

name: Is Alcohol Hand Sanitiser Halal?
note: Yes, most scholars permit alcohol-based hand sanitiser, because it is used for hygiene, not drunk, and the alcohol is usually synthetic or industrial. Mouthwash with alcohol is also permitted by many scholars as long as it is not swallowed, though alcohol-free versions are a simple way to avoid doubt, especially while fasting.
terms: is alcohol hand sanitiser halal? (and mouthwash)

name: Is Smoking or Vaping Haram?
note: Most contemporary scholars say smoking cigarettes is haram because of the proven serious harm to health, and some earlier scholars considered it disliked (makruh). Vaping and shisha are also prohibited or strongly discouraged by most scholars because of nicotine addiction and health harm. Cannabis is haram as an intoxicant.

name: Can Muslim Men Wear Gold?
note: No — wearing gold is haram for men according to all four Sunni schools and the Shia school, based on clear hadith. It is permitted for women. White gold is still gold, so the ruling is the same. Men may wear a silver ring, and most scholars permit other metals such as platinum and titanium.
terms: can men wear a gold ring in islam?
is white gold halal for men?

name: Is Music Haram in Islam?
note: Scholars differ. The majority of classical scholars across the four schools held that musical instruments are prohibited, based on hadith, except the daff (frame drum) on occasions like weddings and Eid. A minority of classical and contemporary scholars permit music whose content is clean. Songs with immoral lyrics are prohibited by all. Vocals-only nasheeds are widely accepted.
terms: can muslims listen to music during ramadan?

name: Can Muslims Keep Dogs as Pets?
note: Most scholars say keeping a dog purely as an indoor pet is not permitted, based on hadith, but dogs for guarding, farming, hunting or assistance (such as guide dogs) are allowed. Touching a dog is not haram; in the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools its saliva is impure and must be washed off, while the Maliki school considers dogs pure. Cats are permitted and loved in Islam.
terms: can muslims keep dogs as pets?
is it haram to have a dog?

name: Is Celebrating Birthdays Haram?
note: Scholars differ on birthdays: some consider them an imitation of non-Islamic custom or an innovation, while many permit a simple family celebration as a cultural custom with no religious meaning. On religious festivals like Christmas, most scholars say Muslims should not celebrate them as religious occasions, but many permit being kind to neighbours, attending family meals and exchanging gifts.

name: Are Video Games and Chess Halal?
note: Playing games is generally permitted if it involves no gambling, no haram content (such as explicit scenes or glorifying evil), and does not make you miss prayers or duties. Chess without money is permitted by many scholars, although some classical scholars disliked it. Card games like Uno are fine without betting.
terms: are video games and chess halal?

name: Can Muslims Marry Non-Muslims?
note: According to the Qur'an (5:5), a Muslim man may marry a chaste Christian or Jewish woman, although many scholars discourage it today. A Muslim woman may not marry a non-Muslim man, according to scholarly consensus. Marrying someone of another faith is not permitted for either. Marrying a cousin is halal in Islam.

name: Chocolate (food guide)
note: Plain chocolate is usually fine: cocoa, sugar, milk and plant emulsifiers. Watch for alcohol in liqueur fillings, gelatine in chewy centres, and emulsifiers such as E471 or E476 whose source is not stated.

name: Sweets & gummies (food guide)
note: Many chewy sweets are made with gelatine, which in the UK is usually from pork. Sweets set with pectin, starch or agar, or labelled halal or vegan, avoid this.

name: Biscuits (food guide)
note: Most biscuits are fine. The usual questions are emulsifiers (E471, E472) from an unstated fat source, whey, and chocolate coatings with the same issues as chocolate.

name: Bread & bakery (food guide)
note: Bread flour, yeast and salt are all halal. Supermarket loaves often add emulsifiers (E471, E472e, E481) that can come from animal fat, and a few bakery products use L-cysteine (E920).

name: Cakes & desserts (food guide)
note: Cakes can contain several things to check: emulsifiers, gelatine in mousse or cheesecake layers, alcohol in soaked or festive cakes, and carmine in red decorations.

name: Crisps & snacks (food guide)
note: Plain and salted crisps are usually fine. Flavoured crisps can contain meat-based flavourings, cheese made with animal rennet, whey, and flavour enhancers that are sometimes made from meat or fish.

name: Ice cream (food guide)
note: Ice cream is often fine, but watch for emulsifiers (E471), gelatine in some premium or soft-scoop products, alcohol in flavours like rum and raisin, and carmine in pink flavours.

name: Yoghurts (food guide)
note: Plain yoghurt is halal. Some fruit and low-fat yoghurts are thickened with gelatine, and some pink ones are coloured with carmine.

name: Cheese (food guide)
note: Cheese depends on the rennet. Microbial or vegetarian rennet is halal; animal rennet is halal only from a halal-slaughtered animal. Parmesan and Grana Padano always use animal rennet.

name: Breakfast cereals (food guide)
note: Most cereals are fine. Check marshmallow pieces (gelatine), flavourings, and emulsifiers. Added vitamin D3 is usually from lanolin (sheep wool), which most scholars accept.

name: Soft drinks (food guide)
note: Most soft drinks are halal. Questions come up about flavourings (which can use tiny amounts of alcohol as a carrier) and a few colours such as carmine in some red drinks.

name: Energy drinks (food guide)
note: Energy drinks are generally halal by ingredients. Taurine in these drinks is synthetic, not animal-derived. The main question some people raise is the flavouring carrier.

name: Sauces & condiments (food guide)
note: Check cooking sauces for wine, mirin or sherry, and for meat stock. Wine vinegar is accepted by most scholars. Some sauces use anchovies (fish), which are halal.

name: Ready meals (food guide)
note: Any ready meal with chicken, beef or lamb is only halal if the meat is certified. Also check for pork, wine in sauces, and flavour enhancers.

name: Sausages & processed meat (food guide)
note: Unless labelled halal, most sausages, salami and cooked meats in UK shops contain pork or non-halal meat. Only buy certified halal processed meat.

name: Pizza (food guide)
note: Pizza raises three questions: the cheese (rennet), the toppings (pepperoni and ham are usually pork), and any meat that is not certified halal.

name: Marshmallows (food guide)
note: Standard marshmallows are made with gelatine, usually from pork. Halal, vegan and some fish- or beef-gelatine versions are widely sold.

name: Chewing gum (food guide)
note: Most chewing gum is halal. Check glycerol (E422), stearic acid and magnesium stearate for an unstated animal source, and the glaze.

name: Instant noodles (food guide)
note: The noodles are usually fine; the flavour sachet is what to check. Chicken, beef and pork flavours can contain real meat extract, and flavour enhancers can be animal-derived.

name: Vitamins & supplements (food guide)
note: The capsule is often the issue: gelatine capsules are usually pork or non-halal beef. Look for vegetarian capsules (HPMC) or halal-certified supplements.

Halal (meaning)
note: Halal means "permissible" in Arabic. In food, it describes what Muslims are allowed to eat and drink under Islamic law.

name: Haram (meaning)
note: Haram means "forbidden" in Arabic: anything Muslims are not allowed to do, eat or drink under Islamic law.

name: Mushbooh (meaning)
note: Mushbooh means "doubtful". It describes ingredients that could be halal or haram depending on their source, such as E471.

name: Makruh (meaning)
note: Makruh means "disliked". It is something discouraged in Islam but not forbidden; avoiding it is rewarded.

name: Zabiha (dhabiha) (meaning)
note: Zabiha is meat from an animal slaughtered the Islamic way: by a Muslim, with God's name, cutting the throat so the blood drains.

name: Tayyib (meaning)
note: Tayyib means "good and wholesome". The Qur'an asks Muslims to eat what is both halal and tayyib.

name: Istihalah (meaning)
note: Istihalah is the complete transformation of a substance into something new, which many scholars say can change its ruling — e.g. wine becoming vinegar.

name: Najis (najasah) (meaning)
note: Najis means "impure". Impure substances such as pork, blood and alcohol (in many views) must be washed off before prayer.

name: Khamr (meaning)
note: Khamr means intoxicating drink, such as wine or beer. It is forbidden in the Qur'an, in small or large amounts.

name: Riba (meaning)
note: Riba means interest or usury. Charging or paying interest on loans is forbidden in Islam, which is why Islamic finance exists.

name: Gharar (meaning)
note: Gharar means excessive uncertainty in a contract. It is one reason scholars debate conventional insurance and some trading.

name: Ahl al-Kitab (meaning)
note: Ahl al-Kitab means "People of the Book" — Jews and Christians. The Qur'an permits their food, which is why scholars discuss kosher meat.

name: BPJPH / MUI (certifier)
note: Halal Product Assurance Organising Agency (with MUI)
terms: halal product assurance organising agency (with mui)

name: IFANCA (certifier)
note: Islamic Food and Nutrition Council of America
terms: islamic food and nutrition council of america

name: HFSAA (certifier)
note: Halal Food Standards Alliance of America
terms: halal food standards alliance of america
